title: Optimal testing of fermionic and bosonic Gaussian states
authors: Vishnu Iyer, Bryan O'Gorman, Ojas Parekh, Kevin Thompson, Andrew Zhao
abstract: We study the problem of property testing quantum states: given a pure state $|ψ\rangle$ that either (A) belongs to some class $C$ of pure states, or (B) is $\varepsilon$-far in trace distance from all states in $C$, determine which is the case with high probability. It is known that there exists classes $C$ for which the sample complexity of property testing necessarily scales with the size of the system. In this work, we identify classes for which testing only requires a size-independent number of samples. We prove a tight sample complexity of $Θ(1/\varepsilon^2)$ for the property testing of five important classes of Gaussian quantum states: 1) Fermionic Gaussian states, 2) Slater determinants, 3) bosonic Gaussian states, 4) zero-mean bosonic Gaussian states, and 5) bosonic coherent states.   While property testers for some of these classes have been studied previously, those analyses only gave upper bounds scaling polynomially in the number of modes. In each case, our tester is the projection onto the ``top'' irrep of two or three copies. We get to constant sample complexity by lower bounding how quickly the rejection probability increases with distance from the class; the main technical component involves bounding the spectral gap of symmetric extension of the test projector. We then establish optimality by proving matching lower bounds based on binary state discrimination for each class. Our testers and optimality claims also extend to the tolerant setting, wherein $ψ$ may be $O(\varepsilon)$-close to $C$ in case (A), rather than lying exactly inside.
summary: This paper develops optimal quantum property testers for several key classes of Gaussian quantum states, including fermionic and bosonic types. It proves that testing membership in these structured classes requires a sample complexity that is constant with respect to the system size, achieving a tight bound of $\Theta(1/\epsilon^2)$. This result is significant because it provides highly efficient verification tools for states common in quantum optics and condensed matter theory.
main_problem: The paper addresses the quantum property testing problem: determining if an unknown quantum state belongs to a specific class of states or if it is far from that class.
main_result: The authors establish a tight, constant sample complexity of $\Theta(1/\epsilon^2)$ for testing five important classes of Gaussian quantum states, independent of the system size.
method: The testers are constructed using projections onto the 'top' irreducible representation of multiple copies of the state, with optimality proven by matching lower bounds derived from binary state discrimination.
model_or_system: The focus is on characterizing and testing five structured classes of pure quantum states: Fermionic Gaussian states, Slater determinants, Bosonic Gaussian states, zero-mean bosonic Gaussian states, and bosonic coherent states.
key_observables: Trace distance ($	ext{dist}(\cdot, \cdot)$), spectral gap of the test projector, and the required sample complexity ($t$).
important_parameters: The error parameter $\epsilon$ (related to the distance) and the number of copies used in the test (2 or 3).
main_assumptions: The analysis extends to the tolerant setting, where the input state may be $O(\epsilon)$-close to the class $C$.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the property testing framework, analyzes the specific Gaussian state classes, develops the projection-based testers, and proves the optimal sample complexity by establishing matching upper and lower bounds.
why_interesting: This work provides fundamental, resource-efficient tools (constant sample complexity testers) for verifying the structure of quantum states relevant to quantum optics and many-body physics, which is crucial for quantum computation and simulation.
